intro: Emma Eames recorded Beach’s Browning song for Victor on 16 March 1905, in D♭ according to the label. She sings the whole song, including both of Beach’s settings of the opening lines, in under a minute.

cues.title: Victor 85057, 16 March 1905
cues.text: Eames recorded the song in New York on 16 March 1905. The first take, made on 20 February, was destroyed. Victor issued take 2 as 85057, with Hahn’s L’Incrédule first and the Beach song second, its key given on the label as D♭. The May 1908 catalogue lists the same coupling as 88008.
cues.evidence: The Discography of American Historical Recordings lists matrix C-2314: take 1, 20 February 1905, destroyed; take 2, 16 March 1905, master, Victor 85057. Its notes say “The year’s at the spring” was sung in English and that the original label of 85057 shows the first selection in the key of A and the second in the key of D flat (https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/200003689). The New Victor Record Catalogue of May 1908, p. 45, lists 88008 as L’Incrédule and The Year’s at the Spring (https://archive.org/details/newvictorrecordc00vict_0); the Discography also lists C-2314 under 88008 (https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/refer/55891).

cues.title: Second setting of the opening lines
cues.text: Beach sets the first four lines of Browning’s poem twice. The first setting, on p. 3 of the 1900 edition, is marked mf and reaches f at “The hillside’s”. The second, on p. 4, restarts a tempo and p and goes on through the rest of the poem.
cues.evidence: The 1900 edition (B♭ version, pp. 3–4): p. 3 opens mf, marks f at “The hillside’s” and slows with poco rall. and rit.; p. 4 restarts a tempo, p, at “The year’s at the spring” and continues to the end of the poem. The sung line of the recording follows both settings in order (https://archive.org/details/per_women-composers-collection_the-years-at-the-spring_1900).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Discography of American Historical Recordings describes the matrix as “Soprano vocal solo, with piano” and names no pianist; the Romophone booklet lists this track among those with piano and gives no accompanist.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Beach’s Browning setting, complete: both settings of the opening lines, then the rest of the poem. It is the second of two songs on one 12-inch Victor side, after Reynaldo Hahn’s “L’Incrédule” (sung in French). The label gives the key of the Beach song as D♭.
fields.note: The pairing, the languages and the key D♭ are documented: the Discography of American Historical Recordings notes that the original label of Victor 85057 shows the Beach song in D flat, and the May 1908 catalogue lists the same pairing. That the track is the whole song is inferred by comparing its sung pitches with the vocal part of the 1900 edition (B♭ version, read in D♭): the leaps to E♭, F and G♭ of the first setting fall in the first twelve seconds, and the restart on p. 4 follows at about fifteen seconds. No source states it, and the D♭ version of the edition has not been seen.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Matrix C-2314, take 2 (the master). Take 1, of 20 February 1905, was destroyed.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: New York, New York, United States
fields.note: Recording place from the Discography of American Historical Recordings; no studio address is given.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Victor Talking Machine Company, Red Seal (12-inch single-faced)
fields.note: The May 1908 catalogue lists the disc on the Emma Eames page at $3.00.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The Discography of American Historical Recordings lists this matrix under 85057 and under 88008, and the May 1908 catalogue lists the pairing with “L’Incrédule” as 88008. The July 1909 catalogue gives 88008 to Eames’s 1908 remake of the song. The Romophone booklet gives 85057.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Both songs are on one matrix, which the Discography of American Historical Recordings titles “L’Incrédule” with “The year’s at the spring” as an additional title and which it notes was “Also recorded as C-6203”, the 1908 remake. The Romophone booklet gives C 2314-2.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Ward Marston, transfers and audio restoration; Ward Marston, producer; Virginia Barder, executive producer. Romophone 81001-2, CD 1, track 5.
fields.note: These credits are printed for the whole set. The Internet Archive item (whose own text gives the set number as 81000-2) names the set and the track but no separate engineer for the file; the person who ripped and uploaded it is not credited as an engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Archive descriptions date the set to 1993; a Beach discography gives 1995, and the booklet scan prints no year. The dates of the disc transfer and the restoration are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 8 April 2025 is a copying event, not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Restoration by Ward Marston for the Romophone CD, with no settings stated; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV or FLAC rip of the CD.
fields.note: The closing chord of this track is D♭ major at concert pitch, within about a tenth of a semitone of A = 440 Hz, which agrees with the key on the original label. Stylus, equalisation and noise reduction are not documented. About five seconds of silence follow the last chord.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Out of copyright: Beach died in 1944 and Browning in 1889.
fields.note: Life-plus-70 terms have run out for both; the first edition was published in the United States in 1900. This covers the song, not modern editions.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US public domain: first published by May 1908 as Victor 88008 (recorded 16 March 1905, issued as Victor 85057). The Archive item carries the Public Domain Mark.
fields.note: Selected under the project’s us-published-before-cutoff rule: a recording first published before 1923 had exhausted its federal term by 31 December 2021. The Discography of American Historical Recordings gives a publication year of [1905] for Victor 85057; the dated catalogue is the source relied on for 1908 as the latest year. The audio is the Romophone restoration by Ward Marston. The Public Domain Mark was applied by the uploader, is a statement by the person who identified the work, and is not the basis for publication. The scanned booklet carries no copyright notice for the transfers (its only © line is for the essay; the tray insert is not in the scan), and the track is one continuous performance in score order. The Ninth Circuit held in ABS Entertainment v. CBS (2018) that a remaster distinguished only by change of medium, declicking or noise reduction generally lacks the originality needed for a new copyright. No source consulted shows Romophone or Marston dedicating the restoration to the public domain, and a claim outside the United States has not been ruled out; the booklet’s text and the set’s compilation are not claimed as public domain.

composer.epithet: American composer and former prodigy from New Hampshire who taught herself orchestration by attending Boston Symphony concerts; known for a symphony built on Irish tunes, first given in Boston.
facts: Piano with Ernst Perabo and Carl Baermann; one year of harmony with Junius Hill; otherwise self-taught

quote.text: I was not allowed to climb up on her lap, or on the music stool. I could only hear music, think music.
quote.source: Amy Beach on her mother’s rule, quoted in Sabrina Clarke, “Amy Beach the Synesthete”, WAM! Women and Music, Rutgers

composer.background:
Amy Marcy Cheney was born on 5 September 1867 in Henniker, New Hampshire, the only child of a paper manufacturer and a singer-pianist. At four she spent a summer on her grandfather’s farm in West Henniker, where there was no piano, and composed three waltzes in her head; she played them when she got home. Her mother would not teach her the piano until she was six. “I was not allowed to climb up on her lap, or on the music stool,” Beach remembered. “I could only hear music, think music.”

The Cheneys moved to Chelsea, Massachusetts, in 1871 and to Boston in 1875. Ernst Perabo and then Carl Baermann, a pupil of Liszt, taught her the piano; Junius Hill gave her a year of harmony. Boston musicians told her parents to send her to Europe. They kept her at home. On 24 October 1883, aged sixteen, she played Moscheles’s G minor Concerto and Chopin’s E♭ Rondo at the Boston Music Hall. Her first song in print, The Rainy Day, a Longfellow setting, appeared the same year. On 28 March 1885 she played Chopin’s F minor Concerto with the Boston Symphony under Wilhelm Gericke.
